text: 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple proves this series isn’t just a cash-grab resurrection. These movies have something to say, and more than ever, we need to hear what they’re telling us.

Leans hard into philosophical territory, contrasting spirituality and scientific reasoning while exploring themes of fascism, survival, and the erosion of identity. This is intellectual horror functioning at its highest level.
Of all the takeaways from this brutal, brilliant film, the biggest is that our understanding of the infected needs to evolve... It might be time for the infected to inherit the Earth
Dr Kelson’s presence elevates the entire film. He provides a change of pace from the horror and brutality, offering both Spike and the audience a resting place at his bone temple.
An atheist and a satanist walk into a bone temple …
DaCosta keeps us off-guard, trying to guess what will happen next and rewarding us for answers more rich and powerful than what we in the audience would have conjured.
A fantastic continuation of the story, Fiennes and Parry are sensational.
Nia DaCosta leaves behind Boyle’s aesthetic for her own, while Garland has the space to develop a more interesting set of characters that triumph on a thematic level.
It's a gory, smart, terrifying look at a dystopia with zombies.

Wildly uneven, but ten times better than its predecessor, The Bone Temple only exists to serve as a stepping stone for the third movie that links back to its original. But this is all Ralph Fiennes. Me, an unabashed Fiennes fan, have no complaints.

A wondrous sequel that is far enough after the franchise’s barbaric start to have the luxury of self-reflection and esoteric rumination, but close enough to the release of its predecessor to swing fresh on the vines.
The direction is bold and redefines the world of 28 Days Later in a way that makes me excited to see the forthcoming fifth film in development.
It's rare for a zombie flick to give the perspective of the zombie. DaCosta provides glimpses of Samson's perspective and of his memories, but, again, it's not nearly enough.
The first great film of 2026 explores what it means to retain your humanity in a world gone mad.
As The Bone Temple barrels towards the inevitable climax, DaCosta builds up one of the most fascinating and intellectually satisfying finales in horror history.
28 Years Later: The Bone Temple is a strange, uneasy, and often frustrating entry in one of modern horror’s most influential franchises.

How's that? Pretty good. Effectively slows down a bit on pace and action, compared to the previous entry, to tell a compelling and sometimes bad-shit crazy set within Danny Boyle's world. Nia DaCosta nailed this one! [Full review in Spanish]

I enjoyed that we spend so much time with Dr Ian Kelson (Fiennes). He's very erudite and humane, which makes for an interesting contrast to the savagery we see elsewhere … There are some magical moments in it as well; it’s not all horror.

Nia DaCosta leaves her mark on the franchise by intensifying the violence and adding brilliant needle drops, while moving away from the lo-fi aesthetic for a more traditional look. A standout performance by Erin Kellyman as Jimmy Ink.
Despite the horror, the gore, and the bloodshed, this must surely be the most optimistic episode (if there is still room for optimism amidst such horror) of the entire saga.
